title: Commits, branches, and the three places
outcome: Draw HEAD, the index, and the working tree before running a command.
cue: Edit here. Stage next. Commit that.
version: Modern Git; check git --version for command availability

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt: A developer stages A, edits to B, commits, and says Git lost B. Explain the state and the command that shows the remaining change.

exercises.title: Change one condition
exercises.prompt: A branch is deleted after a merge. What happened to its commits?

visuals.title: The whole idea, once more
visuals.code:
flowchart TD
 E["Edit file to A"] --> A["Add: index now A"]
 A --> B["Edit file to B: index stays A"]
 B --> C["Commit: HEAD becomes A"]
 C --> D["Working tree still B"]
 D --> F["git diff shows A to B"]
 G["Branch name"] --> H["Commit"]
 H --> T["Tree and blobs"]

trace.title: Working tree
trace.detail: Git stores snapshots and the links between them. A commit names a tree and parent commits. A branch name points to a commit. HEAD normally names the checked-out branch; in detached mode it points at a commit directly.

trace.title: Follow the middle steps
trace.detail:
After add, the index holds A. After editing, the working tree holds B. A commit records A. The remaining A→B difference stays in the working tree.

Draw HEAD → commit → tree → blob, then draw the index as a separate proposed tree. This model explains partial staging, restore, reset, and why a clean diff is not always a clean staged snapshot.

trace.title: Check the result
trace.detail: git diff by itself does not show staged changes. An ignored file that was already tracked remains tracked. Ignore rules affect untracked-file discovery, not all past snapshots.

recallPrompt: Without notes: Draw HEAD, the index, and the working tree before running a command. Give a concrete failure example.
